questions.title: #1 Christ Church
questions.passage:
It is a curious tradition that the clock on the tower of Christ Church Cathedral in Oxford is always five minutes later than standard British time.
The explanation for this lies in the conservative nature of the Cathedral's clergy. It was only when the railways arrived in the middle of the nineteenth century that it became important for clocks throughout the country to be synchronized, however difficult this might be. When the Cathedral was asked to come into line, the clergy discussed the request but decided that this was an idea that needed to prove its worth before being adopted.
questions.question: Why does Christ Church Cathedral clock give a different time from other British churches?

choices.text: Oxford likes to be different from other places.
It was initially a protest against the coming of the railway.
Cathedral staff were reluctant to act too quickly.
It was very difficult to alter the time on the clock.

questions.explanation:
✅ Analysis of the Correct Answer

The correct option is: Cathedral staff were reluctant to act too quickly.

Why this is correct:

  • The passage explicitly states that the reason for the clock's unusual timing is the "conservative nature of the Cathedral's clergy."
  • When the clergy was asked to synchronize, they "discussed the request but decided that this was an idea that needed to prove its worth before being adopted."

This decision to wait and require proof before making a change perfectly aligns with the idea of being "reluctant to act too quickly." The passage attributes the delay not to mechanical difficulty, but to a cautious, deliberative decision by the staff/clergy.

❌ Analysis of the Incorrect Answers

It is crucial in PTE reading to avoid making assumptions about the text. Let's look at why the other options fail:

1. Oxford likes to be different from other places.

  • Why it is wrong: This option is too broad and speculative. The passage does not suggest that the city of Oxford, as a whole, has a desire to be different. The reason given is specific to the clergy's internal decision-making process (their "conservative nature"), not a general civic pride or trend of the city.

2. It was initially a protest against the coming of the railway.

  • Why it is wrong: While the railway prompted the need for synchronization, the passage does not frame the clergy's response as an outright "protest." A protest implies strong opposition. Instead, the text describes a cautious delay—a decision that the idea needed to "prove its worth." This is a measured, conservative approach, not necessarily an emotional protest.

3. It was very difficult to alter the time on the clock.

  • Why it is wrong: This option introduces information that is not mentioned in the passage. The passage focuses entirely on the decision (the clergy's choice to delay the change), not the physical difficulty of the clock mechanism. We cannot assume the clock was hard to change just because the clergy chose not to change it.

💡 Key Takeaway for PTE Success

When tackling these questions, remember this rule: The passage is your only source of truth.

If an option requires you to guess the motivation (like "Oxford likes to be different") or introduces external facts (like "it was mechanically difficult"), it is likely incorrect, even if it seems plausible. Always look for the direct cause-and-effect relationship described in the text!

questions.title: #2 Geothermal Power
questions.passage: Huge reserves of energy have been found in rocks far below the surface of the ground in Britain. It is estimated that the north and southwest regions could hold enough energy in the form of heat to provide power for millions of homes. In fact, up to a fifth of Britain's energy could be provided by this geothermal source. Extracting the heat and converting it into electricity is difficult and expensive. choices.text: to show how common the use of geothermal power is in Britain
to describe the problems related to using geothermal power in Britain
to highlight the potential benefits of geothermal power for Britain
to give a detailed description of how geothermal energy is produced in Britain

questions.explanation:
🎯 Analysis of the Correct Answer

The correct option is: to highlight the potential benefits of geothermal power for Britain

Why this is correct:

  • Focus on Potential: The entire passage is structured around the sheer scale of the energy available. The writer begins with the phrase, "Huge reserves of energy have been found..." and immediately quantifies this potential: "up to a fifth of Britain's energy could be provided by this geothermal source."
  • The Core Message: While the passage does mention difficulties (extraction is "difficult and expensive"), these challenges are presented as obstacles *against* a massive, desirable potential. The writer's primary goal is to make you realize how much energy Britain *could* have, making the potential benefit the central theme.
  • Key Evidence: The phrases "Huge reserves," "provide power for millions of homes," and "keep regenerating indefinitely" all point toward the immense, positive potential.

❌ Analysis of the Incorrect Answers

Understanding why the other options are wrong is just as important as knowing the right answer. It helps you avoid common traps!

1. to show how common the use of geothermal power is in Britain

  • Why it is wrong: The passage does not suggest that geothermal power is common. In fact, it emphasizes the opposite. It states that "Extracting the heat and converting it into electricity is difficult and expensive," which implies that the technology is not yet widely or easily utilized.

2. to describe the problems related to using geothermal power in Britain

  • Why it is wrong: This option is too narrow. While the passage *does* mention problems (difficulty, expense, need for thousands of bore holes), it dedicates equal, if not greater, attention to the massive *benefits* and *reserves*. If the main purpose were only to describe problems, the passage would focus heavily on the costs and difficulties, rather than the "Huge reserves."

4. to give a detailed description of how geothermal energy is produced in Britain

  • Why it is wrong: The passage is descriptive, but it is not a detailed scientific guide. It mentions the need for "Thousands of bore holes," which is a procedural detail, but it does not explain the complex scientific process of heat conversion or energy production in a detailed, step-by-step manner.

💡 PTE Strategy Takeaway

When tackling "Main Purpose" questions, always ask yourself: "What is the single most important idea the writer wants me to walk away with?"

In this case, the writer wants you to be impressed by the sheer amount of untapped energy—the potential benefit—even if the current reality is challenging.

Keep practicing, and remember to look for the overarching theme, not just the facts!

questions.title: #3 Innovation
questions.passage: People tend to think that any new technology or device is an act of genius; something that has required vision and insight to create and then develop into a marketable product. The fact is that innovations were often already 'out there' in the public domain in some form or another. They tend to evolve from notions that have been around for years but that had not, until that point, been suitably adapted. One expert calls this the 'long nose' approach to innovation, whereby new concepts come into the world slowly, gradually revealing all they have to offer.

choices.text: Many new products fail to interest consumers.
New products are not always based on new ideas.

New products are easy to distinguish from old ones.

questions.explanation:
Let's break down the passage, the question, and each option to ensure you understand the logic behind the correct answer.

✅ Analysis of the Correct Answer

The correct option is: New products are not always based on new ideas.

Why this is correct:

This option perfectly captures the writer's main point, which is a critique of the popular belief that all innovations are sudden acts of genius. The passage repeatedly argues that the source of new technology is often pre-existing or adapted.

  • Passage Evidence: The text states, "The fact is that innovations were often already 'out there' in the public domain in some form or another."
  • Passage Evidence: It continues, "They tend to evolve from notions that have been around for years but that had not, until that point, been suitably adapted."

The core message is that innovation is less about creating something entirely new (a "genius" idea) and more about adapting or combining existing, overlooked ideas. Therefore, the main point is that the ideas themselves are not always brand new.

❌ Analysis of the Incorrect Answers

Understanding why the other options are wrong is just as important as knowing the right answer. It helps you eliminate distractors!

1. Many new products fail to interest consumers.

Why it is incorrect: The passage never discusses consumer interest, market failure, or consumer reception. The entire focus is on the origin and development of the idea, not its commercial success. This option introduces information that is completely irrelevant to the text.

2. Creators of new products require a unique set of skills.

Why it is incorrect: This option misinterprets the passage's focus. While the passage mentions "vision and insight," it immediately refutes the idea that this requires a unique, singular genius. Instead, it suggests that the required skill is often the ability to adapt or combine existing concepts, rather than generating a wholly unique idea from scratch. The passage is about the idea's source, not the creator's skill set.

3. New products are easy to distinguish from old ones.

Why it is incorrect: This option directly contradicts the passage's description of the innovation process. The passage describes the "long nose" approach, where concepts come into the world slowly, gradually revealing all they have to offer. This suggests a subtle, gradual evolution, making them difficult to distinguish from their older, foundational forms, rather than being instantly obvious or radically different.

💡 Summary Tip for PTE Reading

When faced with a "Main Point" question, always ask yourself: "What is the author trying to convince me of?"

In this case, the author is trying to convince you that the myth of the "genius inventor" is wrong, and that innovation is a process of adaptation. This realization leads directly to the correct answer!

B-15 broke off from the Ross Ice Shelf in Antarctica. It was the largest iceberg ever documented, with a surface area of more than 4,200 square miles — more than twice the size of the state of Delaware. After it started breaking up, the largest of its pieces, B-15a, drifted along the coast of Antarctica, lingered on a shallow seamount, and collided with an ice tongue, before running aground and breaking again. Late in 2007, the largest remaining chunk floated out into the South Pacific where, in the warmer water, it began to disintegrate.
For the whole of the next year, the ocean was noisier than usual. All the way up past the equator, 4,350 miles or so away from where B-15a broke apart, hydrophones that scientists from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) had suspended underwater were picking up strange signals. Another set of hydrophones, this one in the Juan Fernández Islands, off the coast of Chile, picked up the noise, too, even louder. When the scientists used the two sets of data to determine the source of the noise, they found the most likely culprits: B-15a and C-19a, another giant iceberg.
Twenty years ago, not so long before B-15 broke off from Antarctica, “we didn’t even know that icebergs made noise,” says Haru Matsumoto, an ocean engineer at NOAA who has studied these sounds. But in the past few years, scientists have started to learn to distinguish the eerie, haunting sounds of iceberg life — ice cracking, icebergs grinding against each other, an iceberg grounding on the seafloor — and measure the extent to which those sounds contribute to the noise of the ocean. While they’re just now learning to listen, the sounds of ice could help them understand the behavior and breakup of icebergs and ice shelves as the poles warm up.
